chart.reason: The story is fundamentally about cross-regime numerical comparisons, so charts are the central evidence.

image.reason: Three atmospheric images to break analytical density: empty pandemic street (hook), megaphone metaphor (turn), archival clinic (history). Capped at 3 per instructions.

video.reason: No specific event to re-enact; the story is structural and statistical, not anecdotal.

audio.reason: Dataset is mobility / regime / epidemic counts. There is no sonic dimension and a sonification of regime gaps would feel decorative rather than explanatory.

interactive_or_map.reason: Section 4 (country dots) has a natural geographic and exploratory dimension; section 2 benefits from filtering by month/category.

des_teaser.label: Teaser hero image — empty pandemic street

content.prompt: Editorial photograph, top-down view of an empty city street at dusk during pandemic lockdown, deep shadows, single warm streetlamp glow on wet asphalt, no people, no cars, restrained and atmospheric, cinematic, muted teal and amber palette

des_teaser.brief: Full-bleed atmospheric image of an empty pandemic-era street. The image is the visual manifestation of the dataset's central object: a population that has stopped moving. No text overlaid in the asset itself; headline is rendered as HTML over a dark gradient.
des_teaser.rationale: A still image carries pandemic memory better than abstract iconography; dark editorial tone matches the gravity of the topic.

des_01.label: April mobility gap — diverging bar chart

content.interaction: hover tooltip shows exact percentage drop and the gap in pp

des_01.brief: Horizontal bar chart for April 2020 with one row per Google mobility category. Each row shows two bars side-by-side (democracies in blue, non-democracies in red), bars extend leftward from zero (because values are negative, i.e. drops from baseline). The Retail & recreation row gets an annotation arrow pointing at the gap.
des_01.rationale: A grouped horizontal bar chart is the cleanest way to show five paired comparisons in one read. The diverging-from-zero direction makes the magnitude of the drop physically obvious.

des_02.label: Hook stat callout — 13.7pp

content.label: larger drop in retail & recreation mobility, democracies vs autocracies, April 2020

des_02.brief: Oversize stat callout immediately under the hook lede: the number '13.7' in 96px serif italic, with a small superscript 'pp' and one-line caption beneath. Sits inside the prose column, breaking up the opening paragraphs.
des_02.rationale: The single number that powers the whole piece deserves to be displayed once at full size — it makes the rest of the prose more compressible.

des_03.label: Filterable mobility grid — month x category x regime

content.initial_state: Small-multiples grid: rows = mobility category, columns = month (March/April/May), each cell shows two horizontal bars (democracies, non-democracies) with the gap visible.
content.trigger: Reader can click a month tab at the top to highlight that column, or click a category to highlight that row. A toggle lets readers switch from 'mean' to 'mean ± 90% band'.
content.transition: Highlighted cells get full opacity; non-highlighted cells fade to 30% opacity. The 90%-band toggle adds whisker lines to each bar.
content.payoff: Reader sees the gap is not category-specific or month-specific — it's everywhere, monotonically.

des_03.brief: 5-row by 3-column small-multiples grid of paired-bar charts. Each cell is compact (about 200px x 80px). Tabs and a toggle above the grid let readers explore. All 30 datapoints from ana_03 are visible at once; interaction is for emphasis only, not for hiding data.
des_03.rationale: 30 paired comparisons would be overwhelming as a single chart. Faceting them gives the eye 15 cells to scan; interaction lets readers test the claim that the gap is universal.

des_04.label: Stringency vs mobility — the divergence chart

content.interaction: static; annotations point at each pair

des_04.brief: Two side-by-side panels share a y-axis baseline. Left panel: two vertical bars showing Stringency Index — democracies 79.3, autocracies 80.6 (visually almost equal). Right panel: two vertical bars showing workplace mobility drop — democracies -48.1%, autocracies -38.9% (visually far apart). Annotations: 'On paper: same' over the left panel, 'In practice: different' over the right.
des_04.rationale: The whole point of the section is the contrast between two near-identical numbers and two very different ones. Putting them side by side is the only way the contrast registers visually.

des_05.label: Mobility drop by stringency band — grouped bar

content.annotation: country counts shown as small numbers above each bar
content.interaction: hover shows n, mean drop, and gap

des_05.brief: Three groups on the x-axis (Low / Mid / High stringency band), each containing two bars (democracies blue, non-democracies red). Y-axis is mobility drop, going down from 0. The High band bars dominate visually with the largest gap (13.8pp).
des_05.rationale: This chart is the answer to 'maybe democracies just have stricter laws'. Showing that the gap survives within each band defeats that explanation in one image.

des_06.label: Concept illustration — same megaphone, different listeners

content.prompt: Conceptual editorial illustration, two side-by-side identical megaphones, one painted in soft democratic blue and one in muted authoritarian red, both pointing at a stylised crowd, but only the blue megaphone causes the figures to actually walk away. Minimal flat-vector illustration, subtle paper grain, white background, no text

des_06.brief: A small illustration placed between des_04 and des_05, used as a section break. Provides a moment of pacing relief between two analytical charts. Sized at 60% of column width, centered.
des_06.rationale: This section is heavy with charts and abstract reasoning. A single conceptual illustration breaks the rhythm without diluting the argument.

des_07.label: Interactive country scatter

content.initial_state: Scatter plot, x = stringency (0-100), y = workplace mobility change (% from baseline, with 0 at top, -100 at bottom). 60+ country dots colored by regime (democracies blue, autocracies red). Default view shows all dots at full opacity.
content.trigger: Hover a dot → tooltip with country name, ISO3, regime, exact stringency, exact mobility. Click a regime in the legend to fade the other.
content.transition: Outliers (Japan, Sweden, Tanzania, Belarus) are pre-labelled with leader lines.
content.payoff: Reader sees: at any horizontal position, blue dots tend to sit lower (further drop) than red dots. Japan and Sweden, low-stringency democracies, are visible as the right-kind-of-exception that proves the compliance argument.

des_07.brief: Country scatter (about 60 visible points; full table has 110, filtered for legibility). Pre-labelled outliers are Japan, Sweden, Tanzania (TZA), Belarus (BLR), Ecuador, Bolivia, India, Italy. Trend lines per regime are shown as faint dashed regression curves. Axis from 0 to 100 (stringency) and from 0 to -90 (mobility). Style: clean grid, light gridlines on the y-axis only.
des_07.rationale: The country-level cloud is genuinely explorable; readers want to find specific countries. A scatter is the right form. Outlier labels deliver the editorial points (Japan, Sweden) without the reader having to hunt.

des_08.label: Historical clinic atmospheric image

content.prompt: Black and white archival-style photograph, a vintage 1980s style epidemiologist in a field clinic in sub-Saharan Africa, holding a clipboard, faded paper texture, documentary photojournalism, no text

des_08.brief: Used as the chapter-break header for the historical section. Black and white, narrow band across the page width, sets a different time and tone before the EM-DAT chart. Image alone — caption rendered separately.
des_08.rationale: The shift from 2020 mobility data to 60 years of epidemic history is a major mode change in the piece. A single B&W image is the lightest-weight way to mark that transition.

des_09.label: Decadal medians chart — democracies vs autocracies

highlight.crossover: around 1990s — non-democracies overtake democracies and stay above

content.interaction: hover shows exact median and decade

des_09.brief: Two-line chart (democracies blue, autocracies red), x = decade from 1960s to 2010s, y = median deaths per outbreak. Lines cross around 1990; from then on, autocracies' line stays above. A subtle vertical band marks the crossover decade.
des_09.rationale: A line chart is the right form for a six-decade trend. The crossover is the visual story; the marker calls it out without text.

des_10.label: Closing pull quote — 'will anyone listen?'

content.label: the question for the next pandemic

des_10.brief: Large italic serif pull quote, centered, no chart. Marks the final argumentative beat of the piece without adding more numbers.
des_10.rationale: Closing on a number would be wrong; closing on the question the piece raises is the right editorial move.

page_rhythm.tone: dark editorial — newspaper-of-record style, restrained, analytical
page_rhythm.text_visual_pattern: prose-then-chart with two image breaks (hook image after teaser; megaphone illustration between two analytical charts; B&W clinic at the historical chapter)
page_rhythm.anti_sameness_notes: No audio cards, no scrollytelling waterfall, no dashboard grid. Charts are restrained two-color (blue/red) with annotations rather than legends. Three distinct image moods (atmospheric color, flat illustration, B&W archival) keep the imagery non-repetitive.
page_rhythm.typography_notes: Headline serif (Playfair / similar). Body in a readable serif (Lora) at 18px. Stat callout 96px serif italic. Pull quote 36px italic serif. Section dividers are 1px hairline rules with 32px vertical padding.
